text:
The Long Way Home: Apollo 13

On April 11, 1970, a Saturn V rocket lifted off from Kennedy Space Center carrying three American astronauts toward the Moon. Jim Lovell, the commander, had already flown on Gemini and had circled the Moon on Apollo 8. Fred Haise, a test pilot, was on his first spaceflight as lunar module pilot. Jack Swigert, the command module pilot, had joined the crew only days before launch. The original pilot, Ken Mattingly, had been exposed to rubella, and doctors judged that he might fall ill during the mission. Their destination was Fra Mauro, a hilly highland region that no Apollo crew had yet reached. It was the third landing attempt in the program.

For the first two days, the flight went according to plan. The spacecraft had two main parts. The command module, named Odyssey, was the cone-shaped capsule where the crew would sit for launch and return. Behind it was the service module, which carried the main engine, the fuel cells that generated electricity and drinking water, and the tanks of cryogenic oxygen that fed them. The lunar module, Aquarius, rode docked in front, ready to carry two men down to the surface.

On the evening of April 13, about fifty-six hours into the flight, the crew ran a routine procedure. Periodically, they stirred the supercold oxygen in the tanks with small internal fans to keep it evenly mixed. Swigert threw the switch. A few seconds later, a bang shook the spacecraft. Lights flickered and alarms sounded. Swigert radioed Houston with the line that became famous: "Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here." Lovell, looking out a window, saw a cloud of white gas streaming from the service module into the dark.

Investigators later traced the failure to oxygen tank number two. Months earlier, during ground testing, the tank's heaters had been powered at a higher voltage than they were designed to handle. The heating damaged the wiring and insulation inside the tank. When the fan was switched on that night, a short circuit ignited the insulation in the pure oxygen environment. The fire blew the tank apart and damaged the second tank and its plumbing. Within minutes, most of the service module's oxygen was venting into space. The fuel cells depended on that oxygen, so they lost power one after another. The command module was rapidly becoming a dead spacecraft.

In Mission Control, flight director Gene Kranz and his team had to decide quickly what to do. The priority was survival, not landing. The crew abandoned Odyssey and moved into Aquarius. Aquarius had been built to support two men on the surface for about forty-five hours. Now it had to keep three men alive for roughly four days, and it had to serve as a lifeboat. Odyssey was shut down to save its remaining battery power for the final reentry.

Apollo 13 had been planned on a "free-return" trajectory, a looping path that used the Moon's gravity to swing a spacecraft around the far side and send it back toward Earth. This meant the crew could come home without a large engine burn. Even so, they would need to use Aquarius's descent engine for short corrective burns to steer. On April 15, they passed behind the Moon, roughly 250 kilometers above the surface, and lost radio contact for a time. When they emerged, they were on a homeward path.

Their most urgent problem was carbon dioxide. Like every spacecraft, Apollo used canisters of lithium hydroxide to absorb the carbon dioxide that the crew breathed out. Aquarius had enough canisters for two men. With three men breathing inside it, carbon dioxide levels began climbing toward dangerous levels. The problem was worse because the canisters from Odyssey were square, while Aquarius's receptacles were round. Engineers in Houston worked out an adapter using only the materials on board. The crew assembled it from plastic bags, cardboard from a flight plan cover, duct tape, and a sock, following instructions radioed up from the ground. It worked.

Power and water were scarce, so the crew shut down almost every system they could. Aquarius was not built to be heated for days. The temperature inside dropped toward freezing. The crew wore heavy clothing, and moisture from their breath condensed on the walls and dripped from the ceiling. Water was rationed sharply, which meant the men were thirsty and tired for most of the trip. Lovell later wrote that the cold and the lack of sleep were nearly as hard to manage as the technical problems.

Getting home also meant bringing Odyssey back to life. Its systems had been powered down for days, and its batteries had to be reactivated for reentry. Engineers and astronauts in Houston worked out a careful power-up sequence without knowing for certain how much charge the batteries had left. On April 17, the crew fired Aquarius's engine for a final course correction. Shortly afterward, they separated Odyssey from the service module and saw the damage for themselves. A panel of the service module had been blown away, exposing its interior. The command module's heat shield was intact, however, and that mattered more.

Reentry depended on a precise angle. If the spacecraft came in too steeply, the deceleration would be crushing and the heat too intense. If it came in too shallow, it could skip off the atmosphere and drift back into space. The crew held the course, and the parachutes deployed as planned. At 1:07 p.m. Eastern time on April 17, 1970, about 142 hours after launch, Odyssey splashed down in the South Pacific a few miles from the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima. Lovell, Haise, and Swigert were alive and, for the first time in days, dry and warm in the recovery ship's care.

The mission did not land on the Moon, but the crew's journey set a record. Apollo 13 traveled about 400,000 kilometers from Earth, the farthest any human beings have ever gone. The accident investigation produced changes to the oxygen tank design, to ground testing procedures, and to how spacecraft wiring was checked. Apollo 14 flew to Fra Mauro in early 1971 to complete the mission that Apollo 13 had been unable to finish.

The story is often told with a line that the flight director supposedly shouted, "Failure is not an option." In fact, Kranz did not say those words during the mission. They were written for the 1995 film Apollo 13, which dramatized the flight. The real story needs no embellishment. Three men, a crippled spacecraft, a lifeboat built for two, and a ground team that improvised solutions one problem at a time brought them home.
